title: Chapter 105 — Does the Whale’s Magnitude Diminish?—Will He Perish?
paragraphs: Inasmuch, then, as this Leviathan comes floundering down upon us from the headwaters of the Eternities, it is fair to ask whether, in the long course of his generations, he may have shrunk from the original bulk of his ancestors.

But when we look into it, we find that today's whales are not only bigger than those whose fossil remains turn up in the Tertiary system (which covers a distinct geological period before man), but that among the whales found in that Tertiary system, the ones from its later formations are larger than the ones from its earlier formations.

The largest by far of all the pre-Adamite whales dug up so far is the Alabama one mentioned in the last chapter, and its skeleton was under seventy feet long. Yet we have already seen that the tape measure gives seventy-two feet for the skeleton of a large modern whale. And whalemen have told me that Sperm Whales nearly a hundred feet long at the time of capture have been taken.
But may it not be that while the whales of the present hour are an advance in size upon those of all previous geological periods, they have degenerated since Adam's time?

We certainly must conclude so, if we are to believe the accounts of gentlemen like Pliny and the ancient naturalists in general. For Pliny tells us of whales whose living bulk covered acres, and Aldrovandus of others that were eight hundred feet long — whales the size of ropewalks and Thames Tunnels! And even in the time of Banks and Solander, Cooke's naturalists, we find a Danish member of the Academy of Sciences recording certain Iceland Whales (reydan-siskur, or Wrinkled Bellies) as one hundred and twenty yards long, that is, three hundred and sixty feet. And Lacépède, the French naturalist, in his detailed history of whales, right at the start of his work (page 3), gives the Right Whale as one hundred meters, or three hundred and twenty-eight feet. And this work came out as recently as A.D. 1825.

But will any whaleman believe these stories? No. The whale of today is as big as his ancestors in Pliny's time. And if I ever go where Pliny is, I, a whaleman (more of one than he was), will make bold to tell him so. Because when the Egyptian mummies buried thousands of years before Pliny was even born do not measure as much in their coffins as a modern Kentuckian in his socks; and when the cattle and other animals carved on the oldest Egyptian and Nineveh tablets, by the relative proportions in which they are drawn, just as plainly prove that the high-bred, stall-fed prize cattle of Smithfield not only equal but far exceed in size the fattest of Pharaoh's fat cattle — then, in the face of all this, I cannot understand how of all animals the whale alone should have degenerated, and I will not admit it.

But yet another question remains, one often debated by the more learned Nantucketers. Given the almost all-seeing lookouts at the mastheads of the whale-ships, now pushing even through Bering Strait and into the remotest secret drawers and lockers of the world, and the thousand harpoons and lances darted along all the continental coasts, the disputed point is whether Leviathan can long endure so wide a chase and so remorseless a slaughter; whether he must not at last be exterminated from the waters, and the last whale, like the last man, smoke his last pipe and then himself evaporate in the final puff.

If you compare the humped herds of whales with the humped herds of buffalo that, less than forty years ago, covered the prairies of Illinois and Missouri in their tens of thousands, shaking their iron manes and scowling with their thunder-clotted brows over the sites of what are now crowded river cities, where the polite broker now sells you land at a dollar an inch, that comparison would seem to offer an unanswerable argument that the hunted whale cannot escape rapid extinction.

But you have to look at this question from every angle. It is true that only a short time ago — less than a full lifetime — the buffalo of Illinois outnumbered the people of London today; that now not a single horn or hoof of them is left anywhere in that region; and that the cause of this astonishing extermination was the spear of man. Even so, the very different nature of the whale hunt absolutely rules out so inglorious an end for the Leviathan. Forty men in one ship who hunt Sperm Whales for forty-eight months think they have done extremely well, and thank God, if they finally bring home the oil of forty fish. By contrast, in the days of the old Canadian and Indian hunters and trappers of the West, when the far west (in whose sunset suns still rise) was an untouched wilderness, the same number of men in moccasins, over the same number of months, riding horses instead of sailing ships, would have killed not forty buffalo but forty thousand and more — a fact that could be backed up with statistics if necessary.

Nor, rightly considered, does it seem to be any argument for the gradual extinction of the Sperm Whale, for example, that in former years (the latter part of the last century, say) these Leviathans were met in small pods much more often than at present, and that as a result the voyages were not so long and were also much more profitable. Because, as has been noted elsewhere, those whales, influenced by some considerations of safety, now swim the seas in immense caravans, so that to a large degree the scattered solitaries, yokes, pods, and schools of other days are now gathered into vast but widely separated, infrequent armies. That is all. And equally mistaken seems the idea that because the so-called whale-bone whales no longer haunt many grounds that once abounded with them, that species too must be declining. For they are only being driven from promontory to cape; and if one coast is no longer enlivened with their spouts, then, you may be sure, some other and remoter shore has very recently been startled by the unfamiliar spectacle.

Furthermore, these last-mentioned Leviathans have two firm fortresses which, in all human probability, will remain forever impregnable. And as the frosty Swiss, when their valleys were invaded, retreated to their mountains, so, hunted from the savannas and glades of the middle seas, the whale-bone whales can at last take refuge in their polar citadels, and diving under the ultimate glassy barriers and walls there, come up among icy fields and floes, and in a charmed circle of everlasting December defy all pursuit by man.

But as perhaps fifty of these whale-bone whales are harpooned for every one cachalot, or sperm whale, some philosophers of the forecastle have concluded that this positive slaughter has already very seriously thinned their battalions. But though for some time past a number of these whales, no fewer than 13,000, have been killed every year on the northwest coast by the Americans alone, there are considerations which make even this fact of little or no weight as an opposing argument in this matter.

Natural as it is to be somewhat skeptical concerning the abundance of the more enormous creatures of the globe, yet what shall we say to Harto, the historian of Goa, when he tells us that at one hunt the King of Siam took 4,000 elephants; that in those regions elephants are as numerous as droves of cattle in temperate climates? And if these elephants, which have now been hunted for thousands of years by Semiramis, by Porus, by Hannibal, and by all the successive monarchs of the East — if they still survive there in great numbers, there seems no reason to doubt that the great whale may far more easily outlast all hunting, since he has a pasture to roam in that is precisely twice as large as all Asia, both Americas, Europe and Africa, New Holland, and all the islands of the sea combined.

Moreover, we have to consider that since whales are thought to live a very long time, probably reaching a hundred years or more, several separate adult generations must be alive at any one time. We can quickly get some idea of what that means if we imagine all the graveyards, cemeteries and family vaults in creation giving up the living bodies of all the men, women and children who were alive seventy-five years ago, and then add that countless multitude to the present human population of the globe.

For all these reasons, then, we consider the whale immortal in his species, however perishable as an individual. He swam the seas before the continents broke water; he once swam over the site of the Tuileries, and Windsor Castle, and the Kremlin. In Noah's flood he despised Noah's Ark; and if the world is ever to be flooded again, like the Netherlands, to kill off its rats, the eternal whale will still survive, and rearing up on the topmost crest of the equatorial flood, spout his frothing defiance to the skies.
